newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil high court backs pay rise.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil high court backs pay rise.

text.p: Following are comments from economists and traders on Brazil's high court ruling to grant a 28.9 percent pay rise to 11 civil servants, who argued they deserved the same pay rise received by the armed forces in 1993. Brasilia fears the high court will later rule that the pay rise must be extended to all federal employees.

THOMAS MALAGA, economist at Brazilian retail bank Unibanco: "My impression is that it will necessarily be extended to all civil servants because there is no way they can discriminate against some groups and not others."
"In this case, it will mean further deterioration of government accounts and it complicates the fiscal adjustment," he said.

Malaga added that civil servants would probably get together this year to bring one large case against the government, which would likely be allowed to pay the estimated $7.0 billion in back pay hikes over a period of five years.
"If the government is able to get administrative reforms approved this year, which will cut payroll costs over the next few years, then they will be able to counteract this ruling," he said.
ANDRE PEREIRA, stock trader at Sao Paulo brokerage Corretora: "This had a very bad impact on the market (which fell a total 2.6 percent on the news). It really surprised us.

"But we still don't know if this is going to have a big effect on the public accounts because we need to know how many other workers will benefit by it and how long the government has to pay them," Pereira said.
A sovereign debt trader at a large international bank in Brazil said Brazilian fixed-income instruments fell sharply on the ruling.
"This was definitely not good news," said the trader, who requested anonymity.

He said Brazil's 8-7/8 percent global due 2001 widened 12 basis points to 230 bps over U.S. Treasuries immediately after the ruling. Brazilian C bonds were off a full point at 80-5/8 in late afternoon Brady trade.
